homelab.title: HomeLab
homelab.description: The Linux box under my desk. It runs 19 self hosted services that my family and I use every day, from passwords and shopping lists to fitness tracking and a retro game library.
bullets: Every service is a small Docker Compose stack behind a single Caddy reverse proxy
No port forwarding. Local DNS at home, Tailscale everywhere else
Runs things I wrote myself: a bot that reviews my GitHub pull requests with static analysis, and another that answers League invites in my friends' group chat
This website is served from it through a Cloudflare Tunnel
homelab.alt: HomeLab dashboard showing the status of every service

homelab-status.title: Homelab Status
homelab-status.description: Live status of my home server, served from the edge. A collector on the server pushes a heartbeat every 30 seconds to a Cloudflare Worker, which stores it in D1 and serves it as JSON for this site and as an SVG card for my GitHub profile.
bullets: Push instead of pull. Nothing in the homelab is exposed, the collector only sends HTTPS requests out with a bearer token
Failures are detected by silence. After 180 seconds without a heartbeat the server counts as offline, and the Worker keeps answering with offline since HH:MM
D1 keeps the latest snapshot, the minutes with a heartbeat per day for availability, and hourly CPU and RAM averages for the 24 hour chart. A daily cron clears old rows
GitHub does not run JavaScript in a README, so the profile card is an SVG drawn by the Worker
Fits the free tier with room to spare: about 2,880 requests a day, and an ingest less than 15 seconds after the previous one gets a 429
homelab-status.alt: Architecture of homelab status: the collector on arroz pushes to a Cloudflare Worker with D1, which serves this site and the GitHub README

habitwar.title: HabitWar
habitwar.description: HabitWar turns habit building into a multiplayer competition. Challenge your friends, keep your streaks alive and climb the leaderboard.
bullets: Live on iOS and Android, with paying customers on both platforms
Habits are proven with photos, timers and location
Full product: auth, subscriptions, push notifications and home screen widgets

portobox.title: Porto Box Cup
portobox.description: The official platform of Porto Box Cup, the largest boxing tournament in the world.
bullets: Public event site, a team dashboard for registrations and an admin dashboard that runs the entire event
348 registered teams and more than 1,200 athletes

minix.title: Minix Boxing
minix.description: A two player boxing game for MINIX, written in C with a team of four for Computer Laboratory at FEUP. It runs on device drivers we wrote ourselves: keyboard, mouse, video card, timer and real time clock.
bullets: One player fights on the keyboard, hitting Q W E R prompts as they appear. The other fights on the mouse, clicking bubbles before they close
Perfect timing fills a combo bar, a miss costs you HP, and the timing windows shrink every round
Character select, pause menu and a leaderboard, drawn at 1024x768 in 16 bit colour

about.title: About Me
about.description: I'm Afonso Lima, a Computer Engineering student at the Faculty of Engineering of the University of Porto. Right now my focus is on self-hosting and open source development, I run my own services on Linux and Docker on a home server, and that's where most of my free time goes. Before that I built HabitWar, a social competition app for iOS and Android that's still live, and I work on web and mobile with React Native, Swift, TypeScript, and PostgreSQL. I also write C, C++, Java, and Python. Outside the digital world, I'm a national boxing champion, an important part of my background and identity.
